evidence_cards.title: MEPS 2016: people with a reported ICD-10 A69 (other spirochetal infections, which includes Lyme disease)
evidence_cards.definition: People with at least one condition record whose 3-character ICD10CDX equals A69.
evidence_cards.method: Sum of unique-person weights (PERWT16F) over the domain; standard error by Taylor linearisation over VARSTR/VARPSU. Person-level, one year only.
comparability: A69 is the broad category that contains Lyme (A69.2x); MEPS public files keep only the first 3 characters, so this is NOT a Lyme-specific count and must not be read as Lyme prevalence.
MEPS panels overlap across adjacent years: never add or pool these yearly totals.
Condition rows come from household reports coded by professional coders.

AHRQ (MEPS team, 2026-09-24) urges caution forming Lyme cost estimates from MEPS: pooling 2016-2024 gives only about 300-400 observations, expenditures are highly skewed (about 1,000 or more are needed for a solid mean), only treated Lyme is identified (zero-expenditure cases drop out, biasing upward), events may be flagged as arthritis without naming Lyme, comorbidities cannot be separated from Lyme, and onset dates are not recorded. Lyme-specific A69.2 is available only in restricted data centers.

uncertainty.note: Small samples give very wide, unreliable intervals.

evidence_cards.summary: 2016: about 436,208 people (95% CI 250,739 to 621,678; 31 sampled persons) reported a condition coded A69.
evidence_cards.how_to_use: Cross-check or population context only, never a prevalence of Lyme or Long COVID; not a cost estimate (events are counts, not dollars).

spec.title: Lyme Disease Diagnosis Frequency: Claims-Based Estimate vs. Surveillance Counts
spec.boundary: This simulator models only the case-frequency correction pipeline reported in Kugeler et al. (CDC dispatch, using 2010-2018 MarketScan commercial insurance claims data): a standardized, age-corrected count of people diagnosed and treated for Lyme disease, adjusted by a correction factor for missing diagnosis codes, compared against the much smaller national surveillance case count. It does not include dollar costs, treatment duration, diagnostic delay, caregiving burden, or productivity loss, because the source document reports none of these. The claims-based estimate is built from privately insured US residents under 65 (MarketScan) before standardization to the full US population, so it does not directly represent Medicare, Medicaid, or uninsured populations. The document states that the gap between its estimate and surveillance counts reflects an unseparated combination of real underreporting and clinical overdiagnosis/overtreatment; this simulator preserves that ambiguity rather than resolving it.

takeaway.patient: This CDC analysis of insurance claims suggests that far more people are diagnosed and treated for Lyme disease each year than appear in official health department counts. At the default numbers shown here, the claims-based estimate is much larger than the surveillance total, but the study itself says it cannot tell how much of that gap is real infections that never got reported versus diagnoses and antibiotic treatment given to people who may not have actually had Lyme disease. The study also found that diagnoses in lower-risk states made up a larger share of insurance-based diagnoses than they do of official surveillance cases, which the authors say might partly reflect overdiagnosis, but they are explicit that they cannot confirm this from their data alone.
takeaway.care: This study indicates that the real clinical volume of Lyme disease diagnosis and treatment may be substantially larger than what state surveillance systems capture, partly because medical records often omit the Lyme-specific billing code even when a patient met surveillance criteria, and partly because presumptive (empiric) treatment in practice leads to some unquantified degree of overdiagnosis and overtreatment. The study also found that diagnoses identified through claims data are proportionally more concentrated in low-incidence states than surveillance cases are, a pattern the authors note but cannot fully explain.
takeaway.policy: The study estimates that approximately 476,000 people per year (2010-2018, 95% credible interval 405,000-547,000) were diagnosed and treated for Lyme disease nationally based on standardized, corrected commercial claims data, compared with about 35,000 cases per year captured through national passive surveillance - roughly a 14-fold difference at the document's own default figures. The authors attribute this gap to a combination of true underreporting and clinical overdiagnosis/overtreatment that their data cannot separate, and note that claims-based diagnoses are proportionally more concentrated in low-incidence states (about 19%) than surveillance cases are (about 5%).

patient: If you or a family member were diagnosed and treated for Lyme disease, this research suggests many such cases nationally do not show up in official state or national health statistics, even though the diagnosis and treatment were real.

If you live somewhere not usually considered a high-risk area for Lyme disease, you could ask your clinician in plain terms what symptoms and findings supported your diagnosis, since this study found diagnoses in lower-risk states make up a larger share of insurance records than of official surveillance cases.

Consider sharing this finding with patient advocacy groups interested in how Lyme disease testing and diagnosis practices vary by region, since the study itself says it cannot determine how much of the gap reflects missed real infections versus overdiagnosis.
care: This finding may be worth checking against your own practice's coding habits: the study found that fewer than half of reviewed records meeting surveillance criteria for Lyme disease actually contained the Lyme-specific diagnosis code, which could affect how your own caseload is reflected in claims or registry data.

The study notes that presumptive (empiric) antibiotic treatment for suspected Lyme disease 'inevitably' produces some degree of overdiagnosis and overtreatment, though it does not quantify how much; this pattern may be worth reviewing against your own diagnostic and treatment protocols.

## Parameters and Sources
All figures come from Kugeler et al. (CDC Emerging Infectious Diseases dispatch), using IBM MarketScan commercial insurance claims data, 2010-2018, identifying Lyme disease via ICD-9-CM code 088.81 / ICD-10-CM code A69.2x combined with qualifying antibiotic prescriptions.

- Standardized, age-corrected annual count (default 205,000 patients/year, page 617) already incorporates a 1.25x adjustment for MarketScan's exclusion of people 65 and older. The 150,000-260,000 exploration range is an assumed bound, not from the source.
- Undercoding correction factor (default 2.33, page 617) is based on review of only 672 medical records across New York, Maryland, and Minnesota studies, where just 43.0% of records meeting surveillance criteria contained the Lyme-specific code. The authors flag this as a key source of uncertainty since it more than doubles the standardized count. The 1.5-3.5 exploration range is assumed.
- Surveillance-reported cases (default 35,000/year, range 30,000-40,000, pages 616 and 618) are confirmed/probable cases meeting the national surveillance case definition, reported via passive surveillance, 2010-2018.
- Low-incidence-state diagnosis shares (19% claims-based vs. about 5% typical in surveillance, page 618) compare where diagnoses geographically occur in each data source.

## Calculation
The main output multiplies the standardized count by the undercoding correction factor, following the document's own two-step derivation. At default values this computes to roughly 477,000-478,000, slightly different from the document's own stated headline figure of about 476,000, because the document's internal arithmetic used unrounded intermediate values rather than the rounded 2.33x factor applied here.

## Limitations
This estimate is derived entirely from insurance claims and ICD coding. Because medical records frequently omit the Lyme-specific code even for patients meeting surveillance criteria, any claims-based count - even after correction - likely still undercounts actual diagnosed-and-treated cases, and the correction itself rests on a small 672-record sample from only three states.

The pooled national estimate (about 476,000/year and its components) has not been checked within this document for variation by sex, age, or race/ethnicity; the authors state such breakdowns are reported in a separate companion paper. Federal survey data sources such as NHIS and BRFSS generally support this kind of disaggregated analysis even though this document did not perform it.

Separately, this document describes a systemic evidence-infrastructure gap: medical records and coding systems often fail to capture the Lyme-specific code even when clinical criteria are met, passive surveillance substantially underreports actual infections, and presumptive treatment in clinical practice leads to some unquantified degree of overdiagnosis and overtreatment. The authors call for improved clinician and public awareness and better electronic medical and laboratory systems to close these gaps.

The document explicitly states that the roughly 14-fold gap between its claims-based estimate and national surveillance counts reflects a combination of real underreporting and clinical overdiagnosis/overtreatment that its data cannot separate; neither figure should be treated as the true number of Lyme infections. MEPS survey data cannot be used to validate or extend this estimate, since AHRQ suppresses the Lyme diagnosis code due to insufficient sample size. No cost, treatment-duration, or diagnostic-delay data are reported anywhere in this document.

## Federal cross-check (computed by the system, not by the AI model)

The model only read these quantities from the document; the comparisons below were calculated in code from federal data files. The federal figures are published or surveyed values; the simulator's own outputs are modeled from the uploaded document.

- Cases reported annually through national Lyme disease surveillance (comparison baseline) (2010-2018 average, the United States): the document reports 35,000; CDC's reported cases averaged 34,973 (confirmed and probable together) (yearly totals ranged 30,158 to 42,743), so the document's figure is within 10% of the CDC confirmed-plus-probable total (+0.1% versus the total). Definitions may differ between the document and CDC surveillance, so a gap is a prompt to check, not an error. Federal source: public health surveillance (surveillance report), 2008-2021; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
- Estimated annual frequency of clinician-diagnosed and treated Lyme disease (2010-2018 average, the United States): the document's estimate of 476,000 is 13.6 times the 34,973 cases CDC received as reported (yearly totals ranged 30,158 to 42,743). Reported cases are a passive-surveillance subset, so estimates from claims or models are usually higher; this shows the size of the gap, not which figure is right. Federal source: public health surveillance (surveillance report), 2008-2021; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
